analysis.one_liner: Makes public colleges tuition-free for working- and middle-class students and nearly doubles the maximum Pell Grant.
analysis.headline: The College for All Act was introduced in June 2023 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal-state partnership to eliminate tuition and fees at community colleges for everyone, and at public four-year colleges for students from families earning up to $125,000 (or $250,000 for married couples). It would fund tuition-free programs at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions, raise the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790 for students at public and tribal colleges, extend Pell Grants to cover living expenses, and expand eligibility to Dreamer students. It also reauthorizes TRIO and GEAR UP programs that help low-income and first-generation students.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and their families who would pay no tuition at community colleges and public four-year schools, no matter their age or immigration status, as long as family income falls under the caps. Pell Grant recipients would get larger awards usable for living costs, and students at historically Black and minority-serving institutions would qualify for tuition-free attendance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public college students and their families

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges through federal grants to states, covering 100% of the cost in the first year and phasing down to 80% federal share by 2028-2029.

Eliminates tuition and fees at public four-year institutions for working- and middle-class students — dependent students in single-parent households earning up to $125,000 or married-parent households up to $250,000, with those thresholds rising with inflation in later years.

Raises the maximum Federal Pell Grant to $14,790 for students at public and tribal colleges for the 2024-2025 award year (roughly double the standard maximum), lets students use Pell funds for living and non-tuition expenses, extends the eligibility window from 12 semesters to 7.5 years, and makes Pell grants fully excluded from taxable income.

Funds private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions to eliminate tuition and fees, and bars for-profit colleges that recently converted to nonprofit status from the program for at least 25 years.

Expands Pell eligibility to Dreamer students and those with DACA, temporary protected status, or deferred enforced departure status, regardless of age or immigration status for the tuition-free programs.

Includes protections against schools simply pocketing the money: states must maintain their own higher-ed funding at three-year-average levels, keep instruction spending from falling, ensure 75% of instruction is by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years, and the bill bans using grant funds for stadiums, administrator salaries, or merit aid.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the grants (the bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' through fiscal 2033). States would also be required to contribute a growing share — up to 20% by 2028-2029 — and to maintain their own higher-education spending at three-year-average levels to keep receiving money.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates open-ended federal funding ('such sums as may be necessary' through fiscal 2033), making the total long-term cost to taxpayers essentially uncapped and subject to enrollment growth.

States must pay an increasing share of the cost (up to 20% by 2028-2029) and maintain prior spending levels even during economic downturns; relief is available only when unemployment crosses specified thresholds, so states in fiscal trouble could face pressure to cut other programs or drop out of the program.

The four-year tuition guarantee is income-capped, so students from families above the thresholds still pay full price at public four-year schools, which some critics argue creates a cliff effect just above the income limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: a student from a family earning under $125,000 could attend any public community college or four-year school tuition-free, and low-income students' Pell awards would roughly double and stretch to living costs. The main cost is federal spending on a scale Congress has not committed to — the bill's own appropriation language is open-ended — plus a mandatory state match that phases in over five years. The bill does include real guardrails against the money being diverted to stadiums, administrator pay, or merit scholarships, which is an honest design strength. The tradeoff is straightforward: a major public investment in college affordability versus its cost to taxpayers and states.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the College for All Act of 2023 on June 14, 2023, joined by eight original cosponsors including Sens. Warren, Markey, Murphy, Blumenthal, Padilla, Welch, Van Hollen, and Merkley.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind on the bill.
Ten Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill over its lifetime; no Republican senator did.
The bill died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No group had to fight for anything: the bill died quietly in committee, so the higher-education status quo continued unchanged. Students and families kept paying tuition and fees, and taxpayers were spared a large new federal commitment that no committee ever weighed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; families keep paying tuition

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on June 14, 2023.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican senator joined.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 14, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 11 supporters were all from the Democratic side of the aisle — an Independent sponsor and 10 Democratic cosponsors out of 48 Senate Democrats — and no Republican cosponsored it; the bill's death in a committee chaired by a Democrat was procedural rather than the product of a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill routes tens of billions in federal grants through state public college systems and ties the money to requirements like maintaining instruction spending and tenure-track faculty, so the money reaches classrooms. Public institutions would gain permanent federal funding, though they would lose tuition revenue and face caps on what they can charge other students.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit HBCUs and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: A dedicated grant program would let these institutions eliminate tuition for eligible students, a direct infusion of federal money into schools serving disproportionately low-income students.

For-profit colleges are excluded from the tuition-free program, and schools that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status are barred for at least 25 years. For-profit colleges charge students tuition funded largely by federal aid, so a free public alternative directly competes with their enrollment.
Tuition-free public college and doubled Pell grants covering living costs would reduce how much students need to borrow, shrinking demand for student loans over time.

States would receive the bulk of federal funding for tuition elimination but must contribute up to 20% of costs by 2028-2029 and maintain their own higher-education spending at three-year averages, with relief only during specified unemployment thresholds.
